To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

inactivation of rulD in wild bacteria has minimal effects on growth and ribosome function, whereas it has major effects in K-12 bacteria carrying the prfB mutation that encodes a threonine in place of the more typical alanines at position 246 of RF2, which is found in wild bacteria.

inactivation of the rluD gene encoding a pseudouridine (ψ) synthase in Escherichia colistrains with an RF2 protein containing a defective threonine at residue 246 has a dramatic effect on ribosome function and bacterial growth.

inactivation of rhuD, which encodes a pseudouriidine synthase responsible in Escherichia coil for the modification of three nucleotides in helix 68 of 23S ribosomal RNA, has minimal effects on growth, protein synthesis, and ribosome function in wild-type bacteria but causes slow growth and defects in protein synthesis and 50S ribosome assembly in E. coli and Salmonella strains carrying an RF2 protein containing a threonine instead of alanine at
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of rluD-encoded pseudouridine synthases in bacterial growth, translation termination, and ribosome biogenesis.
the function and regulation of pseudouridine synthases and the role of pseudouridine modifications in ribosome structure and function.
the role of the rluD-encoded pseudouridylate synthase in Escherichia and Salmonella, which are both members of the gamma subclass of the Proteobacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

inactivation of rhlD in K- 12 strains is not associated with any significant ribosome defects and that the previously reported effects of inactivation of rhuD are due to the presence of a threonine in position 246 of RF2.
the effects of inactivation of rhuD are minimal in wild bacteria, but in E. coli and Salmonella K-12 strains the effects are significant due to the presence of a partially defective release factor 2.
the rluD gene is not essential for ribosome function and that the growth and termination defects previously observed in E. coli rluD mutants are not due to a defect in ribosome function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

inactivation of RluD in E.coli has no effect on growth or ribosome function in wild-type bacteria, but has significant effects in E.coli K-12 strains, which carry the prfB T246 allele, and in which the defective RF2 protein has an especially high affinity for the ribosome, and is therefore especially sensitive to perturbation of its interactions with the ribosome.
the rluD gene is not required in E. coli and S. enterica for normal growth or ribosome function.
the h69 Ψ modifications are not critical for growth and ribosome function in most wild bacterial strains, but they are essential in K-12 E. coli strains carrying the prfB mutation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in E. coli, inactivation of rhuD has little effect on ribosome function, but the slow growth phenotype of E. coli K12 strains can be explained by a defective RF2.
inactivation of RluD in wild bacteria has no significant effect on growth or ribosome function.
inactivation of the rluD gene has minimal effects on growth and ribosome function in wild-type bacteria.
